David Ha, CEO of Sakana AI Intelligence emerges from constraints The T-shirt I’m wearing today has a diagram of world models on it. It was drawn by Professor Jürgen Schmidhuber himself back in 1990. Back then, compute was a million to a billion times more expensive than today, and he had to hand-draw these figures and paste them into the paper. Today we have AI scientists writing papers together with us, but it’s good to be reminded of how the innovations of the 1980s and 1990s led to where we are now. One of my hot takes on social media is that foundation models are among the fastest-depreciating financial assets in the history of mankind. As someone who started an AI company that makes these models, this is a real struggle for me. How does Japan compete with the rest of the world in this space? One of my core beliefs is that AI development is not just about throwing more compute and data into ever-larger models. I believe intelligence emerges from constraints. Modern AI scales through abundance, but biological intelligence emerged from scarcity. Evolution selects for doing more with less. Our brains, our language, and our culture are all proof that constraints drive intelligence. More than ten years ago, I got addicted to studying AI and took on some of the hardest tasks in OpenAI Gym. When I trained a neural network to solve the bipedal walker task, I also constrained the size of the robot and the energy it could use. With these constraints, the AI came up with a small, insect-like walker. What happens when there are no constraints at all? The AI discovered a giant robot with no brain that simply falls over toward the exit. We need constraints for our AI to actually have a brain. Discovering Professor Schmidhuber’s papers For the car racing task, where the agent drives from pixels, I gave the agent a world model, so that it could predict what would happen in the future and represent the world in a latent space. As Jürgen always tells us, I went back to look at what people had done in the past. That’s how I discovered his line of papers on world models, from his 1990 paper on making the world differentiable to his 2015 paper “On Learning to Think.” I found them very inspiring. They bring together many concepts, from algorithmic information theory to artificial curiosity, and that’s where I learned to think of an agent as a controller, C, and a model, M. I then wrote the “World Models” paper together with him, which we presented at NeurIPS. We showed that an agent can actually be trained inside the dream hallucinated by its own world model. These ideas now underpin many modern innovations, from self-driving cars to robotics. Sakana AI’s research and AI sovereignty in Japan In 2023, I co-founded Sakana AI with Llion Jones and Ren Ito. Sakana means fish in Japanese. We believe intelligence is not just about the individual fish; it’s the school, and we take a collective intelligence approach. As a company in Japan with limited resources, we also don’t want to do exactly what everyone else is doing. We want to be the red fish that swims a little differently from the rest. David Ha: "Intelligence is not just an individual fish. It's the school." Our research so far includes the brain-inspired Continuous Thought Machines , PC-ALM , which trains 1,000-layer networks without backpropagation, The AI Scientist, published in Nature this year , and the Darwin Gödel Machine , which brings Jürgen’s idea of the Gödel machine to life with LLMs. So how should Japan build AI amid global competition? I see AI sovereignty in Japan as resting on three pillars. Pre-training: the ability to develop this technology from scratch. Post-training: aligning models with our values, especially the values of Japan. And orchestration: combining our models with the frontier models produced by the rest of the world to push performance further. For orchestration we offer Sakana Fugu , and for post-training, Sakana Namazu . The last pillar is pre-training. We will be starting to pre-train our own models, and our Chief Scientist Takuya Akiba will talk about these efforts later today. Our plan is to pre-train an agent-native LLM and an agent-native world model, have them work together on difficult tasks, and improve them through a self-improvement loop driven by the AI Scientist. This plan doesn’t look that different from one of Professor Schmidhuber’s papers: a controller and a world model working together. With the tools available today, we can build on these great ideas from the past and push the frontier. Keynote | Jürgen Schmidhuber Next, Professor Jürgen Schmidhuber delivered the keynote. Neural networks were invented 230 years ago I’m really proud that David chose to show up in a T-shirt based on a drawing I made back in 1990. Modern AI is based on artificial neural networks. Your brain has about 100 billion neurons, each with maybe 10,000 connections on average. At first the strengths of these connections are random, but through learning some get stronger and some get weaker. That’s how the whole system learns to drive cars, translate languages, and do all kinds of things. Who invented artificial neural networks? Some people think it was someone in America, maybe around 1940, but that’s totally wrong. They were invented 230 years ago, between 1795 and 1805. In 1795, Gauss had exactly what was called a 2-layer linear neural network in the 1990s: weights on the connections between input and output units, adjusted so that the mean squared error on the training set is minimized. Back then it was called the method of least squares. The first to publish it was Legendre, in 1805. This Gauss–Legendre network is the core of what everybody is doing at all the famous companies today. The main difference is that today’s networks are deeper. By the way, the young Gauss became famous in 1801 by predicting the position of the asteroid Ceres after it had disappeared behind the sun. He predicted the next token, so to speak, and he got it right. The roots of deep learning, and Japan Who invented deep learning? It started in 1965 in Ukraine, then part of the Soviet Union, with Ivakhnenko and Lapa. Ivakhnenko’s 1971 paper described an eight-layer network that learned to model the British economy by predicting the next value of a time series. Then, in 1967, a Japanese researcher, Shun-ichi Amari, introduced end-to-end deep learning, with a five-layer network, at a time when compute was billions of times more expensive than today. In 1970, Seppo Linnainmaa in Finland published what is now called backpropagation, used by everyone from Google to Sakana AI. Another great Japanese contribution came in 1979, when Kunihiko Fukushima introduced the first convolutional neural network, which he called the Neocognitron. There is a famous video from 1986 of it recognizing handwritten digits. In 1988, Wei Zhang, working at a lab in Japan, combined Fukushima’s convolutional network with backpropagation, and applied it to character recognition. Zhang also scaled it up in the 1990s. So convolutional neural networks, central to computer vision today, were invented and further developed and scaled in Japan. Since I’m here in Japan, I wanted to point out the essential things that happened in this country in the development of modern AI. Jürgen tracing the roots of modern AI, from Gauss to Fukushima World models and artificial curiosity, 1990 Our own contributions to neural nets came later, starting with this picture from 1990. There’s a little robot and a control network. One of the inputs is labeled R, for reward. The robot has pain sensors, and it receives evaluations of what it is doing as input. This is one essential ingredient of what is now called recursive self-improvement: a system that learns not only to do something, but also learns to improve the way it learns, and to improve the way it improves the way it learns, and so on, recursively. For that, the network must see the evaluations coming from the environment. That was already present back then. Then you add a second network, which looks at the robot’s actions and inputs and tries to predict what will happen next. That’s a model of the world. With a good model, you can plan: you can run mental experiments and choose the action sequences that lead to a lot of predicted reward and little pain. But in the beginning, the model knows nothing. That’s why you immediately need something like an artificial scientist, one that invents its own experiments. A baby does not learn by downloading the World Wide Web. If a baby moves its hand, the incoming video changes, and it learns to predict how. That’s how it learns about physics, how apples fall to the ground, how parents react when it cries. It creates its own data through self-invented experiments. The simplest way of doing this, which I published in 1990, is to have the world model minimize its error while the generative controller tries to maximize the same error. Whenever the controller finds a corner of the environment where the model can still learn something, it gets a reward: the eureka reward for inventing an experiment that tells you something you didn’t know. Many have implemented variants of this, and today this is called a generative adversarial network. I called it artificial curiosity. 1991, the miraculous year Back then, deep learning didn’t really work well. You couldn’t deal with long time lags, where something that happened a thousand steps ago influences something a thousand steps later. So in 1991 we had a whole bunch of papers to solve that problem, and funny enough, they are now the P and the T in ChatGPT. Pre-training: compressing long sequences by predicting the next thing. In the same paper, distilling the knowledge of one neural network into another. And the first Transformer variant. I called it the fast weight controller, but it is exactly what was called the linear Transformer in 2020. It scales linearly. With today’s quadratically scaling Transformer, if you have 1,000 times more text, you need a million times more compute. That is one of the reasons why data centers are so expensive. Also in 1991, my brilliant student Sepp Hochreiter introduced the principle of deep residual learning in his diploma thesis. Consider a very simple unit with a linear activation function and a connection to itself of weight 1.0. When you propagate errors back through time, you always multiply by 1.0, so nothing changes over thousands of steps. That is what enables very deep learning through gradient descent, and it’s the core of the LSTM. Later this led to the first deep residual feedforward network which we published under the name “Highway Network” in May 2015 (and then later “ResNet”). In 1991, nobody was interested in all of this. I once gave a talk at a conference where there was only one person in the audience, a young lady. I said, “Young lady, it’s very embarrassing, but apparently today I’m going to give this talk just to you.” She said, “Okay, but please hurry, I am the next speaker.” But every five years, computers got 10 times cheaper. Today compute is 10 million times cheaper than back then, and that’s why the techniques we published back then are now on all your smartphones. Planning without simulating every detail What David showed in his slide refers to a better way of planning. The naive way is to use the world model to simulate the future millisecond by millisecond. That’s good enough for chess and board games, but it’s not what you should do. When you plan a trip from here to Paris, you don’t simulate your hand grabbing the phone. You think of a few high-level things: call a taxi, go to the airport, check in. You make a compact plan and ignore the details. What I proposed in 2015 is to let the controller send queries into the hidden units of the world model, M. M may have seen all YouTube videos, or have lots of experience with robots. The controller is a learning prompt engineer that learns to address the few internal representations relevant to the current problem, interpret the answers, and change its own behavior. These queries are not in English or Japanese; they are just sequences of number vectors. For simple problems, it’s easier to solve them from scratch, but all interesting, complicated problems will greatly profit from the algorithmic information sitting deep in this huge model. In 2018, I also wrote a paper that collapses the model and the controller into one network through distillation. But the more famous paper of 2018 is the one by David, which showed in great experiments how world models can be really useful in practice. AI beyond the screen Let me put all this into a broader historical context. Much of what I mentioned today happened in Germany and Japan. In 1990, Japan seemed like the land of the future. The six most valuable companies in the world were all Japanese. In 1995, the nominal GDP of Japan and Germany together almost equaled that of America plus China. And in 2002, more than half of the world’s robots were from Japan, and the country with the second most robots was Germany. At the moment, the only AI that works really well is AI behind the screen. Behind the screen, there is a superhuman chess player, a superhuman Go player, a superhuman mathematician. But no robot comes close to what a plumber or an electrician can do, or to what a little boy can do with a football. Physical AI in the real world is not owned by anybody yet. We now see an opening for a robot that can learn, by demonstration and reinforcement, to operate all the existing tools and machines. Once we have that, machines can make more of themselves, and we have an ultimate scaling machine. Then it no longer matters how many people a country has; what matters is whether it has machines like that. I hope that Japan and Germany and maybe a few other robot-oriented countries will lead there, and maybe connect to former glory in this way. Jürgen on the promise of Physical AI The future is bright All the existing trends are working for the little guy, not for the big companies. Forty years ago, I knew a rich guy who had a mobile phone in his Porsche, so he could talk by satellite to another guy with a similar Porsche. Super expensive. Today, everybody all over the world has a smartphone that is much, much better. It’s going to be the same with AI. Every five years it gets 10 times cheaper, and the physical limits of this trend are still far away. Everybody is going to have lots of AIs making their lives longer, happier, and healthier. The future is bright. LLM Development at the RSI Lab | Takuya Akiba After a break, three researchers from Sakana AI’s RSI Lab gave talks. The RSI Lab has three teams: language models (LLM), world models, and recursive self-improvement (RSI). First up was Chief Scientist Takuya Akiba, who leads the LLM team. Chief Scientist, Takuya Akiba From the agent layer to the model layer Sakana AI was founded in 2023, and I joined as one of its earliest members. I’ve worked on a variety of things, and one of our focuses has been the agent layer: assuming strong models exist, and researching how to use them to do interesting things. One example is ALE-Agent , an agent designed to discover strong algorithms for combinatorial optimization. We entered it in live competitive programming contests, and after a few attempts, it took first place against human experts . Another is AB-MCTS , a general algorithm for inference-time scaling that calls language models repeatedly to solve very hard problems. It has been deployed in multiple real-world projects at Sakana AI. Working at the agent layer has been fun and successful. But recently, I think the model layer has become attractive again. Recent open models are very strong, close to frontier models, and good enough for real work. Data, training recipes, and software have become more accessible, so building these models is getting cheaper. Perhaps more importantly, specialization at the model layer has become a very attractive option. With agentic reinforcement learning, we can optimize models end-to-end for our own tools, workloads, and scaffolds, and sometimes these specialized models outperform general ones. This year we released Sakana Namazu , a model based on an open model and post-trained mainly for Japanese users. We reduced geopolitical bias, improved its understanding of Japanese culture, and taught it ways of communicating and thinking that feel more natural to Japanese users. Then, this summer, we launched the RSI Lab, with three teams: language models, world models, and RSI research. I represent the language model team. Sakana Sawara So what’s next at the RSI Lab? Today I’d like to introduce our new language model series, Sakana Sawara. Please note that this is still a provisional name. Takuya Akiba introducing the new language model series "Sakana Sawara" (provisional name) Sawara will be our own language model series, built entirely by us from scratch. With Namazu we focused on post-training existing open models; with Sawara we are expanding into pre-training. It won’t be adapted from any other model, so we have full control over it. And it will be an agent-native language model, designed from the start for agentic workloads such as tool-integrated reasoning, coding, and long-horizon tasks. Sawara will serve two purposes. One is to be the foundation of Sakana AI’s products and solutions. The other is to be the foundation of our RSI research. Because we have full control over the model and the recipes, and every process is fully transparent to us, it will enable RSI research with a broader scope. Unfortunately, I don’t have much to share about Sawara yet, because it is still under development. So today I’d like to talk about how I think about language model development: my strategy. The four features of Sawara LLM development is a research competition Many people would agree that this competition is about using more and more GPUs. That’s 100% true. But many also think GPUs are mainly for scaling, that is, for increasing the number of parameters or pre-training tokens. That is actually a misunderstanding. According to Epoch AI , many groups use only a fraction of their compute for final training runs. At OpenAI, for example, final training runs are estimated to have accounted for only about 10% of R&D compute. A large share goes into trial and error, in other words, research. Language model development is more of a research competition than you might imagine. So what are the key factors in this competition? I’d say progress is the product of two things: compute and research efficiency. Compute is simple. More GPUs means more experiments. Research efficiency is underestimated, but it’s equally important, because the result is the product of the two. It’s about how much we can learn from each experiment. Over the past ten years, I’ve seen a huge difference here between researchers. Some people are very good at designing experiments that give us as much information as possible. Talent density and AI tokens at scale What drives a team’s research capability today? I’d say talent density and AI tokens at scale. It’s 2026, not 2023. Since we published the AI Scientist in 2024, many groups have followed, and everyone now agrees that research is a collaboration between humans and AI. We emphasize talent density over headcount, and I’m confident in my team. It’s the most talent-dense team I have ever seen. Interestingly, this way of thinking leads continuously to RSI. We are already using AI, but it’s probably not our own models. Next time, some part of that AI could be Sawara. Then the next version of Sawara could be developed with the help of Sawara. It depends on how you define RSI, but I’d call this fractional RSI. Hopefully, in the future, Sawara will take on more and more of this process. Roadmap Finally, our roadmap. We are now preparing for training, and we will start pre-training Sawara Small (provisional name) this December. If everything goes smoothly, we will release the weights next spring. We also plan to develop a larger model, Sawara Large (provisional name). Towards Open-Ended Autonomous Discovery Systems | Robert Tjarko Lange Next, Staff Research Scientist Robert Tjarko Lange spoke on behalf of the RSI team. Robert Tjarko Lange on Open-Ended Autonomous Discovery Systems The AI Scientist so far When I started my scientific career, one of my big inspirations was Jürgen’s diploma thesis, on genetic algorithms that recursively refine themselves. That’s how I started working on meta-learning. Today, in 2026, we have much more powerful mutation operators in the form of large language models, which let us autonomously test new hypotheses. Scientific progress drives prosperity, but so far most research has been done purely by humans, without AI assistance. So in 2024, as language models began to follow instructions well, we started building the AI Scientist v1 , a blueprint for automating the entire research pipeline with agents, from ideation and novelty checks to experiments, paper writing, and review. A year later, with v2, we used tree search to orchestrate the stages of the research pipeline, and a paper it generated passed human peer review at a machine learning conference workshop . We obtained ethics approval in advance and communicated closely with the workshop organizers, because we always want to respect the scientific process and maintain integrity. Our latest version, v3, also called the Agentic Scientist, can still run fully autonomously, but it is designed for co-discovery, so that humans can work with it to refine hypotheses. It verifies all claims, runs ablations, and aims to reduce reward hacking. We used v3 to write another paper, which we submitted after checking all the claims ourselves, and it was accepted as a main conference paper at ALIFE 2026. Robert on the milestones of the AI Scientist Broadening the ideation radius So what’s next? Many auto-research systems today are a bit like hyperparameter tuning on steroids. They can rewrite code, but their ideation radius is not how humans do research. We need to move beyond hill-climbing benchmarks and push these systems to do research in a much more diverse way. For inspiration, we can look at Sakana AI’s own structure: the Frontier Intelligence Group (FIG) , where researchers explore interesting, long-horizon hypotheses in an open-ended way. How can we build AI scientists in that spirit, less hill-climbed? Human scientists are biologists, economists, and philosophers. To advance science holistically, we need AI scientists that adapt to different disciplines, gather their own expertise, and improve themselves. Additionally, 80% of my own scientific process is trial and error that never makes it into the final paper. These scientific research traces are largely absent from the LLM training process. We need to explicitly think about how AI systems can internalize the scientific method itself, drawing on ideas like Karl Popper’s falsificationism. Science is inherently a collective endeavor, not a lone genius in a corner. How do we build a world where AI scientists collaborate collectively, and where humans are part of that process too? The technical questions become how to allocate resources, how to assign credit to scientific results, and how to judge whether a contribution is meaningful. Finally, safety is really important. But I think the solution is not to stop AI progress, but to use AI to develop AI safely. Applying AI scientists to areas like mechanistic interpretability or chain-of-thought monitoring can give us not only better systems, but also a better understanding of them. World Models & Physical AI | Stefania Druga / Sebastian Risi The third talk, on world models and Physical AI, was given by Stefania Druga and Sebastian Risi. Why Physical AI in Japan (Stefania) We are very excited to do this work in Japan, because Japan excels at robotics and Physical AI. At the same time, Japan faces big challenges: three out of ten people are over 65. That is both a problem and an opportunity. If we combine the hardware capabilities here with what AI can learn today, we can create better applications for the people who need them most. Sebastian Risi (left) and Stefania Druga (right) Check with a world model before acting in the real world (Sebastian) Robot learning has made great progress over the past ten years. But we still don’t see robots in our households, and as Jürgen said, we don’t have robot plumbers or electricians yet. I think two gaps remain: speed and safety. Approaches that use big LLMs are slow at inference. And even when tasks succeed, 18 to 28% of episodes don’t follow the instructions exactly. Our bet at Sakana for closing these gaps is world models. You check actions with a world model before performing them in the real world, and you only accept improvements backed by actual physical evidence. Physical trials are very costly, so robots need a world model that lets them imagine potential futures. In our architecture, a small vision-language model (VLM), which allows fast inference, proposes plans. The world model takes these plans, predicts states several steps ahead, judges feasibility and causes of failure, and scores how close the plan gets to the goal. Many plans are filtered out by the world model, only a few are tried on real hardware, and the results are used to improve the VLM. Sebastian explaining the improvement loop that combines world models and real hardware But what we want is recursive self-improvement: a system that not only gets better, but gets better at getting better. We connect the Agentic Scientist, the agent-native LLM we are developing, and Physical AI, so that the Agentic Scientist can improve the world model itself, and we feed what we learn from the real world back into the Agentic Scientist to close the loop. To avoid reward hacking, we use a frozen gate with strict criteria: repeated gains across evaluations, statistical evidence, and gains on held-out tasks. And building on collective intelligence, which is in Sakana’s DNA, we are also working on making RSI more effective and safer . Stefania presenting early experiments in world models and Physical AI Early experiments (Stefania) A world model predicts what’s next, but an experiment tells us what actually happens. We want to close the gap between the two and learn recursively. In our first example, in partnership with AIRoA (AI Robot Association), we took a fine-tuned π0.5 policy and tested it in simulation on a Franka robot. At first, the robot couldn’t open a drawer or place objects in it. By repeatedly showing the controller where it failed, we improved it until the robot succeeded. The next step is to test the improved policy in the real world. We have also started working on robots that change their own morphology depending on the task. We create simulations from real robot videos, explore in simulation, which is faster, cheaper, and safer, test the resulting controller on the physical robot, and feed the results back. In a simple example, we went through this entire loop. This doesn’t stop at robotics. I connected a microscope and a set of sensors to Sakana’s Agentic Scientist (v3) to forecast the best lighting conditions for collecting data, and then let the system change the lighting itself. Better experiments lead to better models, and better models lead to better experiments. The world is changing. We are modeling the world, machines are adapting to the world we are modeling, and people are changing as well. We want to design a world where people and machines co-evolve in safe and flourishing ways. Fireside Chat | David Ha × Jürgen Schmidhuber The final session was a conversation between David Ha and Jürgen, moderated by Stefania Druga. David Ha and Jürgen in conversation, moderated by Stefania Druga It started with an email Stefania: How did your “World Models” paper come about? David: I was at the NeurIPS 2016 Deep RL workshop, where Jürgen was giving a talk on his paper “On Learning to Think.” That inspired me to learn more about world models. Then I tried to win OpenAI’s car racing task and implemented one of the world model variants. I sent Jürgen my preliminary results, we agreed to turn it into a proper paper with additional experiments, and we presented it at NeurIPS as an oral presentation. Jürgen: You really have to emphasize that this was all driven by David. And it was not just an oral; it was among the top 2% or so of accepted papers. Stefania: What did you think when you received that email with the car animation? Jürgen: It was one of the most charming emails I’ve ever gotten. Eight years on Stefania: It has been eight years since the paper. How has research on world models evolved, and what surprised you? David: We’re seeing tremendous progress in scaling up world models; they’re now used in self-driving cars. But I’m surprised by the lack of novelty. Humans can arrive at a decision intuitively, with a controller working together with a predictor. Yet in robotics, everyone still seems to run Monte Carlo tree search simulations at every planning step. That’s where I hope our work at Sakana AI, leveraging AI scientists, can help advance world models, especially in Physical AI. Jürgen: The main lesson was: just be patient. Every five years, computers get 10 times cheaper. In a couple of decades we will have another factor of a million, and everything that seems impressive today will seem trivial in hindsight. On the other hand, physical robots don’t evolve as quickly as computers. Thirty years ago, there were pretty decent walking robots in Japan. Today’s robots are maybe three to five times better, not a million times better. Physical AI is a slow game. What it takes to be a researcher now Stefania: Agentic coding has shifted developers’ identity, and now we’re seeing the same with scientists. How should people deal with this change? David: The baseline keeps moving higher. If I applied for a job at any AI company today, including our own, I’d probably fail the interview. Three years ago, we looked for interns who could come up with ideas, implement experiments, and collect results. Now you can ask an AI agent to do that, so we expect interns to think like a professor or a PI. Scientists have to think like meta-scientists, and meta-scientists like meta-meta-scientists. It’s turtles all the way down. But there’s one thing I believe will stand the test of time, and I like to call it vision. An example I often bring up in Japan is Nintendo. Nintendo didn’t chase state-of-the-art performance. They stayed true to their vision of creating fun games, and they didn’t need the best hardware to succeed. As long as we have our own vision and mission, we can use technology to achieve it as the technology improves. Jürgen: It’s interesting to see which kinds of artificial scientists are working. The one that has improved dramatically is the artificial mathematician. Mathematics is deductive: the rules are given as axioms, and you can stay behind the screen and search for a proof or a disproof. Physics is very different. You don’t know the rules of the game. You have to take the raw pixels coming at you and distill a new physical law that wasn’t known before. That’s induction, and it’s much harder. I always claim that the first time an artificial physicist discovers a new physical law will be roughly the same time an artificial musician first creates a melody as good as one of the 100 best melodies in human history. David Ha and Jürgen during the fireside chat Closing Perhaps half of the AI Jürgen has envisioned has been realized through generative AI. The other half, such as artificial scientists that invent their own experiments to understand the world, and Physical AI that works in the real world, has yet to scale. AI research today may look dominated by US and Chinese players competing to scale ever-larger foundation models, but this opportunity is open, perhaps even more so, outside the big labs. Japan is one of the most promising places to pursue it. Sakana AI was founded to build a frontier AI company in Japan, bringing together researchers from around the world and top researchers from Japan. At the RSI Lab , launched in June 2026, we are pursuing next-generation language models starting with Sawara, AI-driven AI research, and, combined with these, research on world models and Physical AI, all at once. Jürgen will continue to provide insight and inspiration for this challenge. We hope this symposium will be one of the starting points for opening up the next era of AI, together with companies and research institutions across Japan. Thank you to everyone who joined us. Sakana AI Sakana AI is hiring across research, engineering, and business, including at the RSI Lab. Learn more about the RSI Lab: https://sakana.ai/rsi-lab/ Open positions: https://sakana.ai/careers/
title: 【開催レポート】Sakana AIシンポジウム：Jürgen Schmidhuberが語るAIのこれまでとこれから、日本から挑む言語モデル・世界モデル・Physical AI

abstract: Redaction summary: As part of this assessment, Anthropic had rights to redact any non-public information in this post. Per our approach to transparency , we had the right to disclose if Anthropic exercised redaction rights, and whether or not any of our findings depended significantly on redacted information. All redactions that were important to our conclusions are described in the report below. Executive summary We agree with Anthropic that catastrophic risks from July 15th models were low, but we think it is plausible that they had crossed their early warning threshold at the time. METR reviewed the “Risks from automated R&D” section of Anthropic’s public August 2026 Risk Report . 1 We conducted this review as part of a high-access assessment of AI R&D acceleration, in which Anthropic shared a private version of the Risk Report along with extensive other non-public data. Alongside this review, we are publishing a holistic assessment of AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic . This was conducted by the same METR employees as this Risk Report Review. Overall, we agree with Anthropic that by July 15th, internally deployed models posed low risk of directly automating R&D in key domains or causing acute catastrophic risks from acceleration of capabilities progress. However, the report’s claim that they had not crossed their early warning thresholds relies on contestable judgment calls that aren’t communicated clearly in the public report. While both METR’s researchers on this project and Anthropic’s relevant staff lean toward it not having been crossed, we think it is plausible that it had been, and we believe the public report overall understates the level of acceleration that was occurring. In this review we first summarize our understanding of Anthropic’s Risk Report , including their threat model, early warning threshold and key claims. We then describe our assessment of these key claims and conclusions. Finally, we share details about the process of this Risk Report Review (further details about the process and access can be found in our holistic review ). Summary of Anthropic’s Risk Report Anthropic’s RSP sets two capability thresholds for “Automated R&D in key domains.” Under Anthropic’s RSP v3.4, the Automated R&D threshold is triggered by either of two conditions: Full Substitution Threshold: If they develop a model that can “fully substitute for our entire set of Research Scientists and Research Engineers, at competitive costs (i.e., within a factor of 5).” 2x Acceleration Threshold: If there is “dramatic acceleration” of the pace of AI progress for reasons that likely relate to the automation of AI R&D. 2 This is defined in further detail in the RSP, but the details are not critical to our critique. (Note that although we give these thresholds names for clarity through the rest of this report, they do not have names in the RSP.) The Risk Report argues the Full Substitution Threshold has not been crossed because models are not currently substituting for humans. The Risk Report argues that models do not currently substitute for all of Anthropic’s staff because, despite the fact that Anthropic is highly incentivized to substitute models for research staff as much as possible, research staff still complete work at Anthropic. “[W]e believe it would be clear to us if models were capable of substituting, even at high cost, for the technical work of our entire research staff, and the fact that we do not perform such substitution even when strongly incentivized to is evidence against our models having this level of capability.” Simply put, Anthropic tries hard to substitute researchers out for models, but researchers are still required. They also present benchmark evidence, but we interpret it as less important and more uncertain than this direct observation. The Risk Report argues the 2x Acceleration Threshold has not been crossed as capability metrics and leading indicators show less than a 2x acceleration, with factors other than AI driving that acceleration. The Risk Report describes three primary lines of evidence that they are not crossing the 2x Acceleration Threshold: Limited acceleration in leading indicators: “Our leading indicators point to a picture of meaningful acceleration starting in early-to-mid 2025, though by less than a factor of 2” Limited attribution of this acceleration to AI: “We are fairly confident in attributing the acceleration in 2025 to factors other than our use of AI models, though we also believe that our AI models have been a key factor in the faster trends continuing through the coverage date.” Weak evidence against a sustained acceleration in AECI: Anthropic reports seeing weak evidence of a one-time jump in AECI attributable to non-AI progress rather than continued acceleration. The Risk Report describes the 2x Acceleration Threshold as an early warning rather than direct evidence of high risk. The August Risk Report describes the 2x Acceleration Threshold as follows: “The risk threshold set out in our RSP—a doubling of the pace of progress beyond pre-AI-acceleration rates, attributable to automation of AI R&D—functions as a potential early warning, rather than evidence that the threat has already materialized.” They do not share a precise threshold that would indicate risk was high, but their threat model describes illustrative scenarios: “The threat: We believe that AI models could, in the next few years, have a broad range of capabilities that exceed human capabilities. In particular, most or all of the work needed to advance research and development in key domains—from robotics to energy to cyberwarfare to AI R&D itself—may become automatable. If this is correct, there could be enormous benefits, but these benefits would come with several distinct but related concerns: Sufficiently rapid progress in some areas of technology could change power structures both within and between nations. For example, if an authoritarian regime built a self-reinforcing lead in AI over the rest of the world, this lead could compound into a major advantage in science and technology—which could in turn translate to very sudden and disruptive advances in the ability to wage war, surveil citizens, and/or wield extremely powerful technology over the long term. If AI models develop dangerous goals while heavily automating R&D in key domains, they may cause unbounded harm—up to and including humanity losing control over civilization entirely—by leveraging novel technology and their access to it. If AI can be used to automate AI R&D itself, the result may be extreme acceleration in AI progress, putting a very broad set of risks on the table, including but not limited to those discussed in this report.” Based on these descriptions and conversations with Anthropic staff, we understand the overall risk designation of “low/medium/high” as being about the risk that models at the time directly enable the kinds of catastrophic concerns described above, not the risk that they cross their RSP threshold (though we believe this could have been made clearer in the report). Anthropic concludes the risk from this threat model on July 15th was “low.” Thus, Anthropic concludes risk is “low” overall, since they believe that: their thresholds are unlikely to be crossed, and even if their thresholds were crossed, this may not be sufficient to cause the kinds of catastrophic risks described in their threat model. This is summarized as: “Low. We do not believe our models meet either RSP criterion for this threat model. However, we are less confident in this assessment than we were in prior risk reports, since our most concrete task-based evaluations have “saturated”—i.e., they no longer capture increases in models’ capabilities—and because we are seeing early signs of potential acceleration.” METR’s assessment We find the Risk Report’s argument that the Full Substitution Threshold had not been crossed broadly compelling. The Full Substitution Threshold Anthropic describes is a high bar, and we agree that they would likely have noticed greater progress on automating their research if their models as of July 15th were capable of this. Similar to Anthropic, our confidence in this claim is much lower than it was in the past due to the lack of high-confidence unsaturated benchmarks demonstrating capability limitations that seem critical for automating AI R&D. The lack of such benchmark evidence makes us more worried that alignment, tooling, oversight or elicitation issues are holding back automation despite the models having obtained or being very close to obtaining the required capabilities. We believe the public risk report’s argument that the 2x Acceleration Threshold had not been crossed to be overstated, and believe it is plausible this threshold was crossed by July 15th. Most relevant researchers at METR and Anthropic lean toward the threshold not having been crossed on July 15th, but we think it is plausible that it had been. We believe the public risk report’s conclusion on the 2x Acceleration Threshold seems overconfident, and relies on judgment calls that aren’t communicated clearly by the public report. In particular, we believe the public risk report understated the evidence for acceleration in both AECI and the leading indicators, and also understated uncertainty expressed in the private unredacted report about counterfactual acceleration. Claim 1: limited acceleration in leading indicators. Public risk report Private risk report “Our leading indicators point to a picture of meaningful acceleration starting in early-to-mid 2025, though by less than a factor of 2.” “At our central estimate of the current rate of [redacted] progress ([redacted]×/yr), [redacted] progress rates have less than doubled even if we attributed all of the observed speedup to AI assistance.” METR’s note on this quote: the acceleration rate implied by [redacted]×/yr is 1.97. The 1.97 figure does not appear in the private report; this is our calculation that combines the report’s estimate of the current rate of progress above with an estimate of the historical rate of progress elsewhere in the private report. We believe a reader of the public report would interpret the phrase “less than a factor of 2” to imply an estimate meaningfully below 2; thus it is surprising that the private risk report’s figures imply 1.97. A better description would seem to be “around 2.” METR’s own analysis of these leading indicators, which was redacted from this report, finds a range of reasonable estimates, between 1.3 and 2.8. We have substantial methodological uncertainty about the correct way to measure these values, which we discussed in the full (unredacted) version of the holistic report. As discussed in that report, Anthropic redacted this discussion. METR’s preferred language for the August 2026 Risk Report: “Leading indicators show substantial accelerations, with rates between 1.3 and 2.8, depending on the definition and time period. We are uncertain how these leading indicators relate to downstream capabilities.” Claim 2: limited attribution of this acceleration to AI. Public risk report Private risk report “We believe our internal AI R&D efforts are significantly faster than they would be without AI assistance, but not yet by a factor of 2 (though we are uncertain and measurement is difficult).” “We are fairly confident in attributing the acceleration in 2025 to factors other than our use of AI models, though we also believe that our AI models have been a key factor in the faster trends continuing through the coverage date.” “Overall we expect that end-to-end growth in [redacted] is slightly less than twice as fast as it would be without AI assistance.” “Our central estimates of the speedup of AI R&D progress relative to an unassisted counterfactual are slightly less than a factor of 2 for [redacted]. … we would guess this is more likely to be an overestimate than an underestimate; nonetheless, we have enough uncertainty that it seems plausible we do exceed this factor of 2 overall.” While the first paragraph does express uncertainty about the overall acceleration, the public risk report seems to imply reasonably high confidence that only a smaller fraction of that is attributable to AI, even through the coverage date of July 15th. Meanwhile, the private risk report describes it as “plausible” that the overall counterfactual acceleration attributable to AI exceeds a factor of 2 by July 15th. Based on the evidence we reviewed in our holistic report, we broadly agree with the private risk report’s assessment of the evidence at the time, though directly estimating counterfactual acceleration is very challenging. METR’s preferred language for the August 2026 Risk Report: “We are fairly confident in attributing some acceleration that occurred in 2025 to factors other than our use of AI models, though we also believe that our AI models have been an increasingly important factor in the faster trends continuing through the coverage date. Based on interviews with research leads and informal surveys, we would guess that the overall AI capabilities progress is still slightly less than twice as fast as it would be without AI assistance. We have enough uncertainty it seems plausible we do exceed this factor of 2 overall.” Claim 3: weak evidence against a sustained acceleration in AECI. Public risk report Private risk report “Claude Mythos 5 lies above the historical score trendline by a similar amount to Mythos Preview, which is weak evidence against a dramatic increase in overall model capability trends over time. Based on limited data, Model 2 (not shown on this figure) appears to be around 1.5 points higher on AECI than Claude Mythos 5, with large error bars (a smaller increase than the one from Claude Mythos Preview to Claude Mythos 5).” “Given that not all of our models are trained end-to-end to maximize intelligence per FLOP (indeed, none of them are exclusively optimizing for this goal), there is a question of how many “effective points” we should consider this [AECI] figure to have, and whether the apparent strong linear trend is as reliable a pattern as it appears.” “The most recent and most capable of these four runs … is involved in the training pipeline for Model 2, but we do not think that model's performance is reflective of the performance we expect from later models derived from this base model (which we anticipate to be more significant improvements over Mythos 5).” The public risk report states that Model 2’s score has large error bars, but does not state the qualification in the private risk report that Anthropic expects higher scores from later snapshots of the same base model. In fact, further snapshots of Model 2 did improve on AECI by about the same amount as Mythos 5 did over Mythos Preview. The public risk report also describes finding weak evidence in favor of a one-time jump in AECI at the time of Mythos Preview, but we disagree with their emphasis on this: At the time, the AECI data was only mildly in favor of a jump, and a continued acceleration could not be ruled out. If we reuse the data that was used in the Risk Report, the estimated acceleration is around 1.5x. After the publication of the Risk Report, Anthropic added data from more benchmarks, which estimates an acceleration of 1.9x using the same set of models. We think relying only on the smaller number of models most directly optimized for maximum capability is simpler and more principled, and does not distinguish at all between the two hypotheses. 3 A continued acceleration in AECI would be more consistent with the continued acceleration observed in the leading indicators. As described in our holistic assessment , we think the evidence since the public risk report points in favor of continued acceleration since October 2025. METR’s preferred language for the August 2026 Risk Report: “Given current AECI data, we cannot confidently distinguish between a one-time jump in capabilities and a continued acceleration. However, given the acceleration in the leading indicators mentioned above, a sustained acceleration seems more parsimonious. Two other factors make the current AECI trends hard to interpret: Some models that make up this AECI trend are not optimized for capabilities alone, which makes it harder to interpret how many “effective points” this trend has. Model 2 has not yet finished training, so we expect to see improved performance from later snapshots. Future AECI measurements will likely clarify if there has been a one-time jump or a persistent acceleration.” Despite this, we broadly agree that direct catastrophic risks due to automated R&D from models on July 15th were low. While we think it is plausible, given the above evidence, that models available by July 15th were providing 2x counterfactual acceleration of AI R&D progress, significantly greater acceleration would likely be necessary to enable the kinds of catastrophic risks described in Anthropic’s scenarios of concern above. We also do not believe models at the time could fully automate AI R&D or R&D in other key domains. We thus agree that these risks were “low” for models available at the time. However, as we describe in our holistic assessment , we expect AI’s augmentation of R&D to continue to grow, and we cannot rule out a substantial further acceleration in the pace of capabilities progress over the next 6 months. This could rapidly lead to “high” risks in these areas. Process details Key terms. Shortly after the beginning of METR’s engagement with Anthropic to write an assessment of AI R&D acceleration, Anthropic asked METR to additionally write a review of their August Risk Report, and METR agreed. The exact scope of the review was never formalized, but mutually negotiated over the course of the engagement. COI disclosure. See METR’s Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic . Contract details. See METR’s Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic . Timeline. August 12: Anthropic begins sharing confidential information with METR. August 14: Anthropic shares the August AI R&D unredacted Risk Report with METR. September 18: METR delivers a first draft of its Risk Report Review to Anthropic for feedback. September 22–October 28: METR iterates on the Risk Report Review. October 28: Anthropic gives final redaction guidance for the Risk Report. October 29: Anthropic approves the redacted report. Other disclosures. See METR’s Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic . AEF-1 checklist. See METR’s Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic . Authors: Tom Cunningham , Nate Rush , Parker Whitfill and Hjalmar Wijk . ↩︎ Quoting from the RSP v3.4, this is operationalized as: “We would consider scenario (2) to have occurred where (a) we observe or expect double the rate of progress [fn1] in AI aggregate capabilities compared to both the rate we’d expect and the fastest rate of extended progress [fn2] we’ve observed in the absence of significant AI contributions to AI R&D and (b) it is plausible that this doubling is substantially attributable to the automation of research and/or engineering (as opposed to other factors, such as increased headcount, compute, or general productivity), such that continuation of the trend in AI progress seems likely to lead to even greater acceleration.” [fn1] “Double the rate of progress” means “as much progress in one year as one would see in two years at baseline.” For example, if baseline progress involved a 3× scaleup in compute and a 3× improvement in algorithmic efficiency (for a 9× “effective scaleup”), “double the rate of progress” would entail something like an 81× effective scaleup. This is not the same idea as “doubling researchers’ productivity,” since doubling inputs does not necessarily double the rate of progress. [fn2] Over at least three model generations. ↩︎ We did a naive extrapolation based only on the small number of models most directly optimized for maximum capability, assuming continued acceleration. This extrapolation led us to more correctly forecast future AECI scores, compared to an extrapolation based on all the points. ↩︎
title: Review of the "Risks from automated R&D" section in Anthropic's Risk Report (August 2026)

abstract: Redaction summary: As part of this assessment, Anthropic had rights to redact any non-public information in this post. Per our approach to transparency , we had the right to disclose if Anthropic exercised redaction rights, and whether or not any of our findings depended significantly on redacted information. While we were able to freely share our highest-level conclusions about risk, Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative for these conclusions. Anthropic described the redactions as “aimed at removing confidential information that could accelerate other AI developers.” 1 Some of these redactions are themselves challenging to describe clearly without revealing sensitive information we have been asked to redact. We share a table of important evidence we were and were not able to discuss given the redactions in our process section below. All redactions that were important for our conclusions are covered by our descriptions in that table or other in-line descriptions in the report below. Much of the redacted evidence we viewed had multiple plausible interpretations, and both METR and Anthropic researchers have significant uncertainty about how to synthesize the evidence into a holistic picture. This makes it hard for the public to judge this evidence themselves, reconcile it with evidence from other sources, and come to their own conclusions (i.e. this report does not achieve ‘transparency about evidence’ ). As a consequence, the public has to rely on METR’s judgment much more than would be ideal, given the weight of the questions answered here. Executive summary From August 12 to October 29, 2026, METR staff performed a high-access evaluation at Anthropic to assess the degree to which AI is accelerating AI R&D. 2 If AI systems started to significantly accelerate further AI development, this could lead to a sudden emergence of extreme and risky capabilities . Anthropic offered unprecedented access to internal data on their AI R&D process, including a variety of metrics on pretraining, reinforcement learning (RL), training compute in each domain, benchmark scores for internal models, AI speedup analyses, forecasts of a future model’s metrics, and interviews with relevant staff. In our first section, we share our subjective conclusions about risk . We now believe that: As of October 2026, Anthropic is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025. This estimate is given with high uncertainty; we would not be surprised if the true acceleration was closer to 1.3x or 3x the historical rate. A majority of this acceleration today is likely attributable to Anthropic’s extensive use of AI to do R&D, though there is significant uncertainty and other causes likely played a large role in acceleration in late 2025. The lack of observed bottlenecks or strong diminishing returns means there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration, though, as we say below, we may be missing important bottlenecks. In our second section we share some of the key empirical findings from our Full Report : Since October 2025, benchmark scores (measured via AECI, Anthropic’s version of the Epoch Capabilities Index) for Anthropic’s models have been growing at an estimated 1.9x the pre-October 2025 rate [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x], implying that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year. We are confident that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the scaling of training compute. Interviews and surveys are consistent with AI usage causing a doubling in the pace of capabilities progress. Anthropic staff self-report dramatic uplift from use of AI systems in interviews and surveys, although these are challenging to interpret. We were told that R&D is accelerated primarily via AI assistance rather than fully autonomous contributions, but there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon. We did not see evidence for significant bottlenecks which would prevent further capabilities progress due to limits on algorithmic progress, training compute, experiment compute, or data in the next 12 months. However, our understanding of the status of different bottlenecks changed several times as we received more detailed information, so we are not confident in our current assessment. Some of the key findings that most informed our conclusions about risk were redacted by Anthropic. In our third section, we describe the assessment process : The scope, setup, and timeline of this assessment. Details of the information shared with METR. Details of what information and evidence we were not able to share given Anthropic’s redactions. Finally, we describe the biggest limitations of our analysis: We could be underestimating capability acceleration if we did not assign enough importance to (1) evidence that some growth rates have further increased recently; (2) further automation of AI R&D tasks leading to a further acceleration in progress; (3) evidence that AECI growth has sometimes understated growth in real-world impact. We could be overestimating capability acceleration if we did not assign enough importance to (1) non-AI factors in Anthropic’s research progress; (2) AECI’s focus on verifiable tasks; (3) reasons why Anthropic’s early growth rate (2023–2025) was unusually low. The remainder of the report goes into detailed discussion of each of the key components. We include appendices with supplemental material. Our subjective conclusions on risk Our conclusions on risk. Independently of this assessment, METR published an October 2026 article proposing a set of high-level questions about AI R&D acceleration we believe the public needs to understand to be able to judge loss-of-control risks from frontier AI development. In this section, we describe how the evidence we reviewed in this assessment changed our subjective conclusions on these high-level questions. Pace of capabilities progress. A significant acceleration of Anthropic’s overall rate of progress would be surprising, since diminishing returns and dependence on compute scaling mean this would likely require remarkable scaling in other inputs. 3 After reviewing the internal evidence, we still have significant uncertainty and internal disagreements on the team, but most METR staff who worked on this project now believe that, as of October 2026, Anthropic is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025. We would not be surprised if the current rate of growth was closer to 1.3x or 3x the historical rate. We have additional uncertainty in how this acceleration translates to broader and less well-specified tasks. The 1.9x acceleration [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x] in the AECI trend since October 2025 described below significantly informed this view, but could be explained by overfitting to the benchmark distribution or otherwise be an artifact of the AECI methodology. On the other hand, we are not confident that AECI would reliably let us estimate recent R&D acceleration, since the data points are lagging acceleration in research and are somewhat sparse. Beyond the AECI evidence, we also saw redacted evidence that significantly informed our view on this question, and made us take this apparent ≈2x acceleration more seriously. It also gave us some indication that acceleration could be above 2x and increasing over time, though we would be surprised if it was significantly higher. Attribution to AI. We looked at a variety of factors that could explain the acceleration we observed, including compute scaling, hiring, data improvements, algorithmic discoveries, and resolving other bottlenecks. As we describe below, we were able to confidently determine that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the rate of growth of training compute. Beyond that, there was not a consensus among Anthropic’s own staff and we did not find decisive evidence. Our overall subjective estimate is that: The acceleration in late 2025 was likely influenced by non-AI factors. We investigated a variety of factors which could have contributed to the observed acceleration in late 2025, but details of many of these factors have been redacted. We guess that a majority (perhaps ≈80%) of the current (October 2026) acceleration is due to AI. This judgment is given with substantial uncertainty, but is based on a variety of lines of evidence on contributions from AI and other causes. We believe AI’s contribution has grown relatively more important over time, and do not think the other factors we investigated would explain the sustained acceleration. The evidence of speedup from the usage of AI we describe below also seems compatible with a large contribution. We illustrate these points below: Our more detailed estimates for the cumulative and instantaneous effects of AI on Anthropic’s rate of progress in AECI, and at various stages of the model training pipeline, were redacted. Bottlenecks to further acceleration. A key concern is that acceleration from the use of AI could start to compound, as the development of more capable models leads to further acceleration. As we describe below, we did not identify any clear bottlenecks (limited inputs that would prevent further growth) or steep diminishing returns to further scaling that would get in the way of such compounding acceleration, though our understanding evolved several times over the course of this assessment, and we have significant uncertainty. Because of this, we believe there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration over the coming year. Key findings In this section, we summarize the key empirical findings from our Full Report that we can describe without revealing redacted information (see the process section for more details on what was redacted). Terminology: We describe growth as annual multiples and acceleration as a ratio of growth rates. We use “acceleration” to refer to an increase in the rate of growth, such that a 2x acceleration means that 2 years of historical progress is made in 1 year. If AECI’s historical trend was 15 points/year, then increasing to 30 points/year implies an acceleration rate of 2 (it takes 1 year to achieve 2 years’ progress at the old rate). For an exponentially growing variable, the acceleration rate is the ratio of growth rates. If a variable is growing 3x/year, then to make 2 years of progress in 1 year the growth rate must be (3 2 )x/yr = 9x/yr (and acceleration can be written as ln(9)/ln(3) = 2). Since October 2025, benchmark scores for internal models have been growing at around twice their historical rate. Benchmark scores of Anthropic’s models, as measured by AECI (Anthropic’s version of the Epoch Capabilities Index ), have accelerated 1.9x [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x] since October 2025. Put another way, Anthropic appears to have made as much progress on benchmarks in the past year as they did between October 2023 and October 2025 (roughly, Claude 2.1 to Sonnet 4.5): Our estimated acceleration is greater than that reported in the Haiku 5.5 system card (1.7x) primarily because of the inclusion of data on newer unreleased models, explained further below. We investigated the robustness of these results to different choices of benchmark inclusion, model dating, model inclusion, and benchmark saturation. Robustness analyses find acceleration rates between 1.1x and 2.9x. We would be surprised if the true evolution of benchmark scores (e.g. as measured by an improved version of AECI) showed no acceleration or acceleration above 3x. See our appendix section for details. The acceleration is not driven by an acceleration in the scale of training compute. We received convincing evidence that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the scale of training compute. Further details on this evidence were redacted. Interviews and surveys are consistent with AI usage driving this doubling in the pace of capabilities progress. We have many lines of evidence relevant to AI’s contribution to progress in different parts of the model training pipeline, including interviews, self-reported uplift, headcount, lines of code, experiment usage, and qualitative reflections from leadership. We highlight three important unredacted sources. First, both METR and Anthropic interviewed many researchers in detail about the degree of overall acceleration in their area of work attributable to AI use (see details in the appendix below). Our overall impression was a quite wide range of estimates, but centered around a 2x acceleration. Some quotes, with sensitive details redacted, are in the appendix. Second, Anthropic also shared data on self-reported uplift due to AI from a variety of sources. The most recent data is from a series of Slack polls, where staff use reactions to vote on their estimated speedup from the most recent model at the time. We consider this to be only very loose evidence, as the responses reflect low-effort consideration. Nevertheless, we observe consistent growth in these self-reports, and very high levels (reaching 12x in October 2026), as shown in the chart below. Note that individual uplift/speedup estimates do not correspond to acceleration rates. Sustaining a particular growth rate in outputs like model capabilities generally requires a similarly sustained growth in inputs like labor and/or labor productivity to overcome diminishing returns. Achieving a significant acceleration in the overall rate of progress generally requires a significant acceleration of these inputs. We thus care most about whether we see a large change in the growth rate of individual uplift, not the absolute level. Our more detailed analysis of what rate of growth in individual uplift might be needed to explain our estimated acceleration rates in key areas was redacted. Third, we understand that AI is not yet able to make highly significant and fully autonomous contributions to the most important parts of the model training process. However, researchers described significant “signs of life” implying such contributions could occur soon, although with substantial variation in maturity depending on the area. We did not identify any convincing bottlenecks to continued rapid progress. We did not see evidence for significant bottlenecks in algorithmic progress, training compute, experiment compute, or data that will take effect in the next 12 months. However, our understanding of the status of different bottlenecks changed several times as we got more detailed information, so we are not confident in our current assessment. Anthropic redacted our analysis of a number of specific bottlenecks. Additional redacted evidence was sometimes hard to interpret, but supports sustained and potentially increasing acceleration. We investigated a number of internal metrics and methodologies for measuring acceleration in key areas of the model training pipeline. Process details METR staff assessed how much AI is speeding up AI R&D at Anthropic. METR staff 4 (2.5 full-time equivalents) piloted a high-access evaluation at Anthropic to assess the degree to which AI is accelerating AI R&D, and how quickly extreme and risky capabilities may emerge in the near future. Anthropic lists AI R&D acceleration as a key risk indicator in its Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP). In this assessment, we do not pay special attention to the thresholds set in the RSP. Instead, we try to develop a holistic picture of AI-driven acceleration of AI R&D. This engagement started in mid-August, and is distinct from the assessment announced on October 15 by Anthropic. Details of the engagement. The METR staff worked over eleven weeks to independently assess how much AI is accelerating AI R&D at Anthropic. Our assessment focused on three broad questions: Has the growth rate of Anthropic’s internal capabilities accelerated? What share of any acceleration is attributable to AI? Are there important bottlenecks that could slow growth or limit acceleration in the near term? We were additionally scoped to review the AI R&D section of Anthropic’s August 2026 Risk Report, which we are publishing separately . As we describe below, the initial contracted assessment was scoped to include a verification of what percent of compute was allocated to capabilities vs. safety. METR had the ability to request access to any information we believed relevant to understanding AI R&D acceleration, and Anthropic could unilaterally approve or reject our requests. In practice, we often negotiated with Anthropic staff and compromised towards data that was informative, not extremely sensitive, and easy to share. We give more details on what Anthropic shared as well as what it declined to share below, noting that broadly the access provided surpassed our expectations. For this engagement, we did not request or receive access to sample from non-public models. Note that neither METR nor Anthropic intended for this project to involve full “employee-like” access, meaning unmediated access to data, documents, or models. Limitations We report our best guesses at ways in which we could be misinterpreting the evidence. We discuss the main ways we could be making mistakes in our interpretation of the evidence. We highlight: Limitations that result from the structure of this assessment. Limitations that result from incorrect analysis. Limited access may have led us to miss important context or data. Despite the access provided to METR, it is clear that staff-level access would enable a significantly deeper assessment. Our pipeline of information was relatively narrow, and a small number of our requests for data were denied. Being able to read documents on demand, observe internal discussion and debate, and have frequent and diverse conversations would have allowed for a richer view. While we believe we had access to the bulk of relevant information, it is possible we missed important information because we did not know it existed or could not look for it ourselves. Over the course of our exercise, we substantially changed our interpretation of key data as more context was shared with us, in some cases leading to multiple reversals on critical questions. We believe fuller access would have dramatically sped up that process of proper interpretation, and we think there likely remain points which we may have misinterpreted due to insufficient context. Acceleration could be higher than this report estimates. Our best guesses as to how we might be underestimating acceleration: We may have missed recent further acceleration. The rate of growth could be undergoing continuous acceleration, e.g. hyperbolic growth. While we do not see clear evidence of this in the AECI trends, there is other evidence that makes this seem more plausible which Anthropic redacted. If growth is hyperbolic, we are likely underestimating instantaneous acceleration and substantially understating acceleration in the near future. In addition, we observe model-level outcomes only after a model is trained, meaning we observe acceleration in effective R&D with a lag roughly equal to the model’s training time. Automation could be closer than we estimated. We understand that AI cannot yet fully automate substantial parts of Anthropic’s model training pipeline; however, there are “signs of life,” discussed below. It is possible that automation is close, and leads to very rapid acceleration once human bottlenecks are removed. AECI could understate real-world capability impact. We have sparse data on the relationship between benchmark scores and real-world impact. As one example, ECI scores on math have not accelerated substantially, but we are now seeing the resolution of Millennium Prize Problems that have evaded decades of human effort. Real-world impacts may be downstream of capability thresholds that models suddenly pass, leading to sudden impacts that are hard to predict. Acceleration could be lower than this report estimates. Our best guesses as to how we might be overestimating acceleration: Non-AI factors could explain most of the acceleration. It’s possible that the non-AI factors explain all or most of the recent acceleration. This implies we have less reason to expect high future growth or future accelerations. Acceleration might be limited to well-specified tasks. Much of the evidence we looked at measures performance on well-specified tasks that are easy to grade automatically or with a language model. If recent models have been growing more quickly on “clean” tasks than on “messy” tasks (relative to historical relative growth rates), then we may be overstating the acceleration in real-world impact. For instance, recent progress may be overfitting to the types of tasks which are included in AECI. Our acceleration numbers could be overstated if the historical rate of growth was unusually low. If progress historically was below its normal or natural rate due to temporary factors, this could lead us to overestimate the amount of acceleration. As we describe in an appendix , Anthropic models had a lower historical growth rate on AECI than the broader industry frontier before late 2025, which could explain some of the acceleration. One graph that shows AECI results for a subset of models chosen on the basis of information that is redacted. Methodological details on AECI estimation. We use Epoch’s public code to estimate AECI values for each model. We generate 95% confidence intervals via bootstrap by drawing benchmark scores with replacement, stratified by model. Our underlying data includes the AECI scores of many snapshots per model. These snapshots differ in both dates and AECI scores. For publicly released models, we include the snapshot that was publicly released and the date that snapshot was available for use by most Anthropic employees. For example, if a model has two snapshots: one available to Anthropic employees on November 10 and one available to Anthropic employees on November 20, and the second snapshot was released publicly on December 1, then our procedure would assign November 20 as the release date. We think there are many reasonable alternative dating procedures (e.g. at first snapshot release instead of last snapshot), which are shown below in one of the robustness exercises. For models that are never released, we include snapshots that received substantial internal usage and the date most Anthropic employees could use them. We use the date at which the model could be used by most Anthropic employees instead of public release dates; this allows us to make apples-to-apples comparisons with unreleased models. These in general show slightly higher degrees of acceleration as Anthropic is holding onto more recent models for slightly longer before their public release. When we fit trends over time we use ordinary least squares with equal weight to each snapshot on the frontier. The confidence interval in the trend estimation only accounts for uncertainty in the AECI scores for each model, and does not include sampling uncertainty over which models are included in the fit. We estimate a learned breakpoint in the trend, though we exogenously impose that there is 1 breakpoint. We estimate the breakpoint is October 7, 2025 in our main AECI specification. For our robustness checks, we maintain this October 7, 2025 breakpoint to ensure comparability. Robustness: Estimates of AECI acceleration vary 1.1x–2.9x depending on the link function.
