This lack of benchmarks which are difficult for Model 4 makes us somewhat nervous about our ability to measure AECI now and in the future. Most of the benchmarks used for Model 4 appear reasonably linear in log-odds space. A specific concern in measuring acceleration with AECI is benchmarks with many broken tasks, or benchmarks with a fat-tailed distribution of task difficulty. The logistic link function assumes exponential tails of task difficulty; if we instead had a fat-tailed distribution of task difficulty, this would mean that going from 98% to 99% requires more AECI points than going from 80% to 90% (the logistic assumes they are approximately equally difficult). A fat-tailed distribution of task difficulty could cause us to underestimate acceleration; as described above, using cauchit or log-log link functions (which model the last few tasks in a benchmark as particularly difficult) results in acceleration estimates of 2.8x and 2.9x, respectively. We perform a simple diagnostic test for task difficulty. For each of the 15 benchmarks used for Model 4 in AECI, we compared a model’s estimated AECI against the model’s log-odds score on that benchmark. If the AECI assumptions are satisfied, meaning task difficulty is logistic in a model’s latent ability, then we would expect each plot to be linear. If there are many broken tasks or a fat-tailed distribution of difficulty, then we would expect these fits to be concave (we would expect a convex fit if there are disproportionately many easy tasks). We noticed there are 3 of 15 benchmarks with notably flat or concave fits. When we re-estimate AECI for all models without those 3 suspicious benchmarks, Model 4’s score increases by 1 point, from 178.6 to 179.7. We thus think there is some weak evidence for fat tails causing understatement in acceleration, but the magnitude is not large. Tokens per benchmark may be too low. Using a low expenditure in benchmarking could bias estimates of capability growth downwards if later models show higher returns to expenditure (i.e. if early models plateau with expenditure, but later models show high returns). Anthropic shared with us data on tokens used on benchmarks in the AECI. A typical task (one attempt) used about 2.5M input and 72k output tokens across internal benchmarks, and about 10M input and 94k output on agentic coding benchmarks. For a loose comparison, Epoch AI uses roughly 0.5M input and 10k output tokens on a typical task across a few public benchmarks (GPQA, AIME, SWE-bench), and 1M input and 8k output tokens on a specific agentic coding benchmark (SWE-bench). For another loose comparison, METR uses roughly 650k output tokens for its latest long-running software benchmarks, though it is possible the token accounting is not comparable. Moreover, it would be informative to see returns-to-expenditure curves for each model, i.e. scores elicited at different levels of expenditure. Anthropic’s system cards do report expenditure curves for some benchmarks (e.g. Opus 5.5 system card ). There is some recent evidence that it is possible to use very large amounts of inference compute to solve difficult problems (e.g. Navier–Stokes ). Overall, our guess is that the AECI scores for each model could be increased by a handful of points if inference tokens were scaled further. Our rough guess is that this would have similar returns across models, so the degree of estimated acceleration would be the same, though this is not something we looked into deeply and it is possible that recent models have better token scaling properties. An acceleration in benchmark scores may fail to track acceleration in real-world impact. Ideally we want to know the real-world value, or potential impact, of each model, not its benchmark scores. If real-world impact is smoothly related to benchmark scores, then we should expect an acceleration in AECI to be associated with an equivalent acceleration in real-world effects. 5 There are a number of reasons why acceleration in AECI may fail to track acceleration in the real-world impact of model capabilities: If real-world impact is a convex function of benchmark scores, e.g. if impact depends on crossing a capability threshold, then AECI would understate real-world acceleration. In some domains we have seen a steady increase in benchmark scores accompanied by sudden accelerations in real-world impacts, e.g. impacts on the rate of discoveries in cybersecurity or math ( ref ). If the benchmarks in AECI cover only a subset of capabilities, and the real-world impact has diminishing returns in those capabilities, then AECI could overstate real-world acceleration. For example, suppose AECI primarily measures a model’s ability to solve formal problems, but there are diminishing real-world returns in that ability; then we might observe an acceleration in AECI without an acceleration in real-world impact. Overall, we are confident there has been at least a modest acceleration in the growth of benchmark scores. We believe there is significant risk that acceleration in AECI may not map cleanly to acceleration in real-world impact. Evidence of AI speedup There is considerable evidence of AI speedup. We define AI speedup as the ratio between a staff member or team’s output with AI and without AI, noting that output can often be difficult to measure or define. Even though this rate of progress by end of year will be even faster … my attribution [mostly not to Claude] and uncertainty remain.” — METR interview “One impact is SWE acceleration, which is extremely substantial. We’re definitely benefiting from that differentially between 2025 and 2026.” — METR interview No Adversarial robustness We believe this exercise was reasonably adversarially robust. As this is an independent assessment, it is important for us to do our due diligence and understand how hard it would have been for Anthropic to systematically mislead us, i.e., how likely it is that we could have been led to an incorrect conclusion intentionally. Adversarial robustness weakness 1: We relied on data from a few Anthropic employees. Most of our data was received through two technical staff members; however, we interviewed around 15 other Anthropic employees on a range of topics. We did not notice any discrepancies between what our primary contacts said and what our interviewees said. Given that many of these Anthropic employees were chosen by us, not Anthropic, we think this would have been challenging to pull off if we were being given purposefully misleading information. Adversarial robustness weakness 2: Most analysis relied on Claude. Claude was involved in many stages of this project, and so in principle could be distorting our perception of the data. We believe Claude was deeply involved in: the majority of data collection and analysis that we received, writing a significant share of the documents we received, the majority of our own analysis. We did not detect any significant discrepancies consistent with a systematic bias even when checking against human interviews. We suspect this is not a significant risk. Overall, we think it is extremely unlikely Anthropic was actively trying to mislead us. However, we believe greater access would allow us to increase the degree of adversarial robustness. Process transparency disclosures COI disclosure. We applied v1.0 of our conflict of interest policy when selecting the team for this project, which was the live policy at the start of this project. At the start of the project, one participating team member was in discussions with Anthropic about a possible role. They received an offer and declined it. This team member also had equity in a competitor as an ex-employee. As such, we required that all of their work incorporated into the assessment was thoroughly checked 6 by an unconflicted team member who took personal responsibility for its accuracy. Going forward, our updated COI policy , applied to risk assessments starting after October 9, 2026, would simply require recusal in such a situation. No one working on this project held equity in Anthropic. Our COI policy requires recusal in the case that a relevant staff member holds equity. (None of METR’s staff hold Anthropic equity, but one incoming staff member does.) We believe there are no other conflicts that would cause a reasonable person not affiliated with METR to have materially less trust in this assessment. Other disclosures. Our process transparency policies require us to describe both the formal constraints (e.g. redaction and publication rights), and any other factors that may have affected our outputs. To mitigate informal pressures, we generally aim to share enough of the relevant evidence for the public to arrive at its own conclusions, but this was made more difficult in this case due to redactions. In order of impact, from highest to lowest: Considering impact on negotiations with other companies and possibility of Anthropic retracting access. These assessments with companies are voluntary and we considered how this output would affect our future ability to do these assessments — for example, if we are too critical of Anthropic for access limitations or making particular redactions, this might make other companies or Anthropic itself less willing to work with us in the future. The biggest effects here are: We want to avoid disincentivizing companies from sharing relevant evidence with us that they then redact the details of, so we try to focus discussion of limitations from redactions on cases where they impacted our ability to communicate our most core conclusions and uncertainties. We avoid more detailed process descriptions that would disincentivize companies from doing exploratory collaborations or would make them feel that they need to have everything locked down and avoid changing their mind or discovering new information while working with us. We instead focus on communicating the aspects of the process that ended up having significant effects on our final output. We made significant clarity edits, particularly to the Risk Report Review, in response to feedback. Our Risk Report Review went through several drafts, partially in response to significant feedback from Anthropic about communication clarity and reducing the surface area for adversarial misreadings of our report. In some cases we felt this feedback toward METR staff was overly forceful, but Anthropic was receptive to our feedback on this point and we hope to develop more detailed processes and guidelines for this in the future. We do not think the final assessment or the Risk Report Review is significantly distorted by this. Summarized contract terms. We summarize relevant contract terms below. Scope Scope. METR independently assesses how much AI systems are automating or accelerating AI R&D at Anthropic. Access rights Anthropic obligations. Anthropic provides the access listed below as reasonably needed, a designated point of contact, and reasonable help arranging surveys and interviews. Anthropic can decline requests that would take disproportionate effort or that fail its information review, but will explain why, describe in general terms what was withheld, and offer alternatives where practical. Access granted to researchers. The contract describes a variety of information that we had access to in previous engagements as a minimum bar for access in this assessment. It also describes logistical details about conversations with Anthropic staff. We describe the access we ended up getting above . Information review process. Anthropic aims to decide on information requests within three business days and provides a point of contact for questions. Publication rights Publicity. Neither party makes public statements about the agreement without the other’s approval, except that both can disclose that the engagement exists and its general nature (an independent AI R&D and compute-allocation assessment). METR publication rights. METR has the following publication rights: Approved public claims. METR submits proposed public findings to Anthropic for review before publication. Anthropic may require redaction of confidential or non-public information, and the parties discuss redactions in good faith, with Anthropic’s redaction requests controlling. METR may submit new or revised claims for clearance at any time. Without further review, METR may publish approved public claims, publicly available information (including previously approved claims, e.g. from the Frontier Risk Report), information derivable from a model or document once it becomes public, and METR’s own analysis or commentary on those. Anthropic can ask METR for a short delay of any public statement, subject to limited exceptions. Transparency. METR can always disclose: the existence and general terms of the review and redaction process whether Anthropic exercised redaction rights whether any findings depended significantly on redacted information the level of access METR received the confidentiality framework. Deliverables A full report: unredacted, delivered to Anthropic, covering the full project scope. A METR-internal report: the full report after light redactions by Anthropic, for sharing with METR staff. [Note: this report was not created during the process for timing reasons.] Public claims: the public report, cleared through the redaction process described under Approved public claims. Independence and conflicts of interest Independence. METR conducts the project and reaches its conclusions independently and does not enter arrangements that would make it financially, operationally, or managerially dependent on Anthropic. METR minimizes conflicts of interest and discloses any that a reasonable person in the industry would consider relevant in public or regulator-facing publications. METR can still evaluate other AI providers. Anthropic will not seek to influence METR’s findings in ways that undermine the project’s integrity, and METR retains sole discretion over methodology and conclusions. No payment. No fees are paid in either direction. Tokens and credits provided to METR assessors are free, and each party covers its own costs. No METR has not established a responsible disclosure policy. Update log November 6, 2026 We made the following changes to the AEF-1 checklist : Removed leftover template notes from items 1.1 and 2.4. Corrected item 1.1 from “Yes” to “No”, and amended its notes accordingly. Indented the sub-item rows. We agree that Anthropic’s redactions were limited to confidential information that could potentially accelerate other AI developers, though most of the redacted information was very high-level. We do not make a comment on whether these redactions were justified overall, since we do not think METR is well positioned to weigh a company’s business interest in preserving this confidential information against the public’s interest in better understanding the risks from AI development. Instead, we focus on describing the nature of these redactions and how they affected our conclusions . ↩︎ Authors: Tom Cunningham , Nate Rush , Parker Whitfill and Hjalmar Wijk . ↩︎ METR has published multiple lines of research relevant to AI R&D acceleration, with results pointing in both directions: our time-horizon trends suggest rapid progress, while our 2025 developer productivity study found early-2025 AI tools caused a slowdown, our estimates of future compute bottlenecks point to limits on scaling, and our analysis of benchmarks overstating AI progress cautions against reading too much into headline scores. ↩︎ Four primary authors worked on this report. Two further METR employees spent time supporting and overseeing this work. ↩︎ A separate problem is benchmarks intended to have an interpretable outcome, e.g. if SWE-bench tasks fail to fit the description of “resolving github issues.” We are using AECI as a black-box index of overall capability, so are not affected by these problems of benchmark description. ↩︎ Per our COI policy, this means following at least the usual quality of review of METR research, entailing understanding the data and analysis well enough to be able to understand the validity of the conclusions, and including consistency checks, understanding the provenance of statistics, and reading through some of the underlying data. ↩︎
